Sake
SāK
n. (rendering Hebrew ma'an and 'ābūr, Greek heneka and dia)
From Old English sacu, a lawsuit, contention, or cause — the same root that gives German Sache, a matter or case. To do a thing for someone's sake was therefore, originally, to do it on his behalf as one would argue his case. The Hebrew l'ma'an means for the purpose of or on account of, and Scripture's most weighty uses of the phrase concern God acting for the sake of His own name.

Biblical Definition

Sake is the word by which Scripture states the reason a thing is done, and its most important use answers the question why God saves. The shepherd psalm does not ground the leading in the sheep's merit: “He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake” (Psa 23:3). The motive is God's own name — His revealed character and reputation — and this is the strongest possible ground of assurance, since a salvation resting on the believer's worth could be lost with it, while one resting on God's name is as secure as God's regard for Himself. Ezekiel puts it bluntly: I do not this for your sakes, O house of Israel, but for mine holy name's sake. The second great use turns the word toward suffering, and the Lord Jesus makes His own name the ground of the last beatitude: “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake” (Mat 5:11). The qualification is exact — falsely, and for my sake — which excludes suffering brought on by one's own folly or rudeness. Paul takes up an old psalm to describe the ordinary condition of the church: “For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter” (Rom 8:36); and he explains what such a life is for: “For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh” (2Co 4:11). The dying of the servant is the means by which the life of the Master becomes visible.

Webster 1828 Definition

Final cause; end; purpose; account — the reason for which a thing is done; and in Scripture the name's sake for which God saves and leads, and the Christ's sake for which His people are reviled and delivered unto death.

expand to see more

SAKE, n. 1. Final cause; end; purpose; or rather the purpose of obtaining. We say, a man labors for the sake of gain.

2. Account; regard to any person or thing. I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake. Gen. 8.

3. Cause; reason; as, for the sake of peace, he yielded the point.

4. In the older sense, a cause or suit at law; contention; whence the phrase for one's sake, on his behalf.

5. In Scripture, he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake. Psalm 23. Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you for my sake. Matt. 5.

Key Scripture

Psalm 23:3 — "He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake."

Matthew 5:11 — "Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake ."

Romans 8:36 — "As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter."

2 Corinthians 4:11 — "For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh."

Modern Corruption

Persecution language is claimed for consequences a believer has brought on himself by rudeness, folly, or partisanship, so that the beatitude's two conditions — falsely, and for Christ's sake — are quietly dropped.

expand to see more

The beatitude of Mat 5:11 is guarded by two qualifications, and both are routinely omitted. The first is falsely: the evil said must be untrue. A Christian who is disliked for being abrasive, dishonest, or careless in his dealings is not suffering reproach for righteousness; he is bearing the ordinary fruit of his conduct, and Peter says as much — let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters. The second qualification is for my sake. Opposition incurred for a political allegiance, a cultural preference, or a personal cause is not persecution for Christ, however sincerely the two are conflated. Where the qualifications are dropped, a genuine comfort becomes an instrument of self-deception, and the church loses the ability to tell a martyr from a nuisance.

There is a corresponding failure in the other direction: a squeamishness that will not admit persecution is normal Christian experience. Rom 8:36 quotes a psalm to describe not an extremity but the settled condition of God's people — killed all the day long, accounted as sheep for the slaughter — and Paul places it inside the chapter that begins with no condemnation and ends with no separation. He does not treat it as a contradiction of God's love but as one of the things that cannot separate us from it. The principle to recover is the purpose stated in 2Co 4:11: the believer is delivered unto death for Jesus' sake that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest. Suffering rightly borne is not merely endured; it is the appointed means by which a watching world sees the life of the risen Christ in mortal flesh.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew l'ma'an means for the sake of, on account of, to the end that; ba''ābūr means for the sake of or because of. Greek heneka is on account of, and dia with the accusative means because of or for the sake of.

expand to see more

Hebrew l'ma'an (H4616) — for the sake of, to the intent that; for his name's sake (Psa 23:3) and for thy servants' sake.

Hebrew ba''ābūr (H5668) — on account of, for the sake of; I will not again curse the ground for man's sake (Gen 8:21).

Hebrew shēm (H8034) — name; God's name being His revealed character, for His name's sake means according to who He has declared Himself to be.

Greek heneka (G1752) — on account of, for the sake of; blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake (Mat 5:10).

Greek dia (G1223) — through, and with the accusative, because of; delivered unto death for Jesus' sake (2Co 4:11).

Usage

"Of the ground of God's dealings: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake (Psa 23:3)."

"Of the qualified beatitude: when men shall revile you... falsely, for my sake (Mat 5:11)."

"Of the purpose of the believer's suffering: delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest (2Co 4:11)."
